title: Not annihilation (section 27)
hookLine: don't think the bodhisattva destroys things; emptiness is not nothing

lines: NOTHING IS REAL, SO NO DISHES.
cards: Somewhere tonight a college sophomore reads one chapter of Buddhist philosophy, shuts the book, and tells the roommate: nothing is real. So the dishes don't matter. The roommate, who has seen the sink, has thoughts.

It's an old wrong turn, and the Diamond Sutra has been walking right past it for weeks: no self, no marks, no merit held, no teaching owned. Keep cutting like that and someone will call the whole thing a wrecking ball.
In section twenty-seven, the Buddha blocks that road by name.

teach.b: The sutra has cut almost everything a person could hold: a self, the bodily marks, merit, the teaching itself, even the raft. A listener could decide the bodhisattva's job is to tear things down.

So, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells Subhuti: don't think the highest awakening was reached through the marks. And let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of anything.
Not of a single thing. The cutting was never demolition. This isn't a new idea dropped in at the end.
In an early discourse, the Buddha tells a monk named Kaccana that everything exists is one extreme, and nothing exists is the other. The Tathagata teaches by the middle, without going to either.
It's the middle way you've met many times on this path, and section twenty-seven stands on the same ground.
When the sutra says a thing has no fixed self, it hasn't said the thing is gone.
Empty, in this teaching, means empty of a fixed, separate core, not empty of being here.

teach.h: EMPTY OF A CORE, STILL HERE.
teach.b: A cup that is only so called still holds the tea. The bodhisattva who frees no beings is still at work helping them. So the roommate is right, and so, in a way, is the sutra.
Nothing is fixed. The dishes are still real. And somebody still has to wash them.

how: Buddhist teachers present emptiness as a middle way between the views that everything exists and that nothing exists, and section 27 of the Diamond Sutra is read as a guard against hearing emptiness as nothingness.

o: the belief that a self survives every death intact
the sutra's cutting never teaches that things are destroyed
the fear that awakening will erase who you are

p: the monk told about the middle

s: the bodhisattva path teaches the destruction of things
section 27 says no one should claim it teaches the annihilation of anything.
the Buddha called 'nothing exists' an extreme
in the discourse to Kaccana, alongside 'everything exists'; he teaches by the middle.
empty means not there at all
empty of a fixed, separate core, not empty of being here.

games.q: after all the sutra's cutting, a friend says: so the bodhisattva path destroys everything. what does section 27 say?
o: no: they don't teach the annihilation of anything
only the bad things get destroyed
games.why: the Buddha says let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of any thing.

practice: Let your attention land on one ordinary thing near you: the chair holding you up, the floor, a plant on the sill. Notice it has no fixed core you could pull out and keep; it's made of other things, and it's changing.
Then notice, just as clearly, that it's here, warm or worn or doing its job, and let both be true at once, maybe with a quiet thank you.

wordCard.voice: Not annihilation. Section twenty-seven: those on the bodhisattva path don't teach the destruction of anything. Empty of a fixed core is not the same as nothing. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: cutting off, annihilation; the extreme section 27 says the bodhisattva path does not teach.

carryVoice: Your line: not nothing. Empty of a core, and still right here. Same time tomorrow.
